title: Anointing of the sick
hookLine: not only for the dying; oil for anyone seriously ill or old (CCC 1514)

lines: A HOSPITAL ROOM, THE DAY BEFORE.
cards: A hospital room, late afternoon. A woman in her seventies is going in for heart surgery tomorrow. Her daughter has called the parish, and a priest comes in with a small oil stock in his pocket, the size of a lipstick.
The daughter looks nervous. Isn't this, she whispers, what they do when someone's dying? The priest smiles.
It's a common mix-up. Her mother isn't dying. She's sick, and scared, and that's exactly who this is for.

teach.b: For a long time this sacrament was called extreme unction, the last anointing, and in practice it was often saved for the very end.
So some people still think of it that way: the priest arrives, and it's time to say goodbye. After the Second Vatican Council, the Church changed the name and the emphasis.
It's the anointing of the sick, and the Catechism says it's for anyone who begins to be in danger of death from sickness or old age. Not dying: beginning to be in danger. Before major surgery.
When a chronic illness gets worse. When age makes a person frail. And it can be received again if the illness returns or worsens.
The roots are in the letter of James.

teach.h: IS ANY MAN SICK AMONG YOU?
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord."
James goes on: the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up.

The priest lays his hands on the person's head in silence, then anoints the forehead and the hands with the oil of the sick, blessed by the bishop. Only a priest can give it. What do Catholics believe it does?
Strength, peace and courage to face the illness, union with Christ's own suffering, forgiveness, and sometimes, if God wills, bodily healing.
It doesn't replace doctors; Catholics go to both. When someone is truly near death, the priest may also hear their confession and give Communion, called viaticum, food for the journey.
Together, those are what people mean by last rites.

how: A Catholic who is seriously ill, frail with age or facing major surgery can ask a priest for the anointing, at home, in hospital, or at a parish Mass for the sick; it can be received more than once.

games.why: the Church gives it to anyone in danger from serious illness or age, and before major surgery. the old last-minute habit is what changed.

practice: Bring to mind one person who is sick, in the hospital, or very old and frail: their face, the room they're in, and what they're afraid of, if you know.
If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, simply keep them company in your mind for the length of the bell.

wordCard.voice: Extreme unction. The old name for anointing of the sick, oil on the forehead and hands, for anyone seriously ill or old, not only the dying. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: olive oil, the word in James 5:14 for the oil used to anoint the sick.

carryVoice: Your line: the sick are not forgotten. Strength for the journey, not only for the end. That's day one hundred thirty.
